## TL;DR

Expanded task creation and editing QA at 375 px, 768 px, and 1280 px. Component tests drive the production drawer’s actual controls and screenshot file input. Headless WebKit measures the rendered drawer with the built global CSS and the compiled scoped styles of both `TaskDrawer` and `TaskDependencyPicker`.

## Work and rationale

The review found that the first layout fixture omitted the dependency picker’s scoped stylesheet. The dependency picker is a child component with its own CSS rules, so loading only the global stylesheet and TaskDrawer CSS could not establish the prerequisite picker’s production geometry. I added its SFC style to the fixture and compile it with the matching `data-v-*` scope ID from the picker’s actual rendered root. The browser page now receives the compiled picker styles alongside the actual drawer markup and global production CSS.

The interaction matrix remains responsible for behavior. At each target width it creates a task by filling the title, choosing priority and area with the visible controls, selecting a prerequisite, attaching a PNG through the screenshot file input, and saving through the mocked repository store. The edit case changes priority, area, and prerequisite through the drawer controls and verifies the patch payload. A separate picker interaction checks selecting and removing the prerequisite.

The WebKit test covers stable geometry. It measures drawer bounds, scroll overflow, and visible control bounds for both create and edit states at each width. It captures the actual production component DOM from Vue, reads the built global UI stylesheet, and compiles the SFC scoped styles using their own rendered scope IDs. It does not use a handcrafted replacement form or copied picker CSS. The QA document now states this method and its evidence limits explicitly.

## Approaches tried

An earlier implementation tried to serve TaskDrawer’s full module graph directly to WebKit. That graph imports server modules with Node built-ins, so a standalone browser entry was impractical. The working approach captures the actual Vue rendered markup in the component environment and measures it in headless WebKit with production CSS. To keep teardown reliable, global styles come from the build output and component styles are compiled directly from their SFC sources; the test starts no Vite dev server.

For scoped styles, I associate each SFC stylesheet with the data scope attribute on its component root. This ensures the dependency picker selectors in the browser page match the same root and descendants as in the app.

## Challenges and blockers

Vue adds the parent component scope to nested child roots as well as the child’s own scope, so selecting the first `data-v-*` attribute in the whole drawer would bind the picker CSS to the wrong ID. The fixture locates the exact `.task-dependency-picker` and `.drawer-wrap.drawer` root tags, then reads the scope attribute on each tag separately. A prior test version also left a temporary Vite server to close after the browser assertions; replacing it with built CSS and direct SFC compilation eliminated the teardown timeout.

Screenshot decoding is asynchronous in jsdom. The create test uses a deterministic FileReader fixture while retaining the real file input change event and production dropzone emit, then waits for the reader callback before asserting upload behavior. The external repository writes remain mocked by design.

## Key learnings

Responsive evidence needs every stylesheet that owns rules for the measured subtree. A component’s DOM can be genuine while its measurement is still incomplete if a child component’s scoped stylesheet is missing. Matching each stylesheet to the rendered scope ID makes that relationship explicit and testable.

Keep browser tests focused on their job: use component tests for state transitions and payload assertions, then use a headless browser for rendered geometry with production styles. QA documentation should describe both methods and avoid implying that mocked repository calls prove live upload or physical device behavior.
